Summary  
This blog-style paper argues that modern society increasingly hijacks innate human reward mechanisms through engineered products (e.g., hyper-palatable foods, loot-box video games), framing the phenomenon as “Adversarial Goodhart” in which external optimizers deliberately drive proxy metrics (dopamine spikes, engagement) away from people’s true goals. It proposes that individuals can learn to “notice the taste of lotus” (become aware of the sensation of reward hijack) and that society can regulate exploitative design or build alignment constraints into AI systems. No formal experiments are reported; evidence is anecdotal and illustrative.  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[78] – Medium-high: the text is short and mostly conceptual, so the main reasoning chains are unambiguous, but interventions had to be moderately inferred and therefore carry lower evidence scores.  

Instruction-set improvement: 1) Clarify how to handle sources with only anecdotal evidence—explicitly permit creating speculative validation-evidence nodes that aggregate such anecdotes. 2) Provide a standard mapping when multiple section titles cover the same idea. 3) Add an allowed edge label “illustrated_by” for anecdotal examples.  

Inference strategy justification  
Because the author offers no concrete empirical studies or step-by-step solution designs, I applied moderate inference (confidence 1-2) to identify plausible AI-safety-relevant interventions—user awareness training, regulatory limits, and adversarial-Goodhart audits—directly implied by the text’s recommendations.  

Extraction completeness  
All concepts needed to connect the central risk (exploitation of human reward circuitry) to the three distinct intervention families are represented and inter-connected. Each node participates in at least one causal-interventional path; no satellites remain. Framework ideas (e.g., “noticing lotus taste” and “adversarial Goodhart”) are decomposed into white-box component nodes.  

Key limitations  
1) Validation evidence is largely anecdotal, so edge confidences are low.  
2) Regulatory and AI-design interventions are extrapolated rather than explicitly detailed in the source.  
3) The short text limits granularity; future richer sources may further refine these nodes.
